lines.text: Your mechanism is built and wired, and Tuner X is already on your laptop. Today they meet. Get this part wrong, and every later lesson is spent fighting the hardware.
Start with the motor. Its controller is built into the back, and it reports its own position so you already have one sensor before you add anything.
So why does the arm get a second one? The motor's own count starts from zero wherever it sits at boot. This encoder reads a magnet on the shaft, and it remembers the angle with the power off.
The CANivore is the reason you don't need a robot yet. Your laptop plugs into it over USB, and it carries the conversation to everything else.
If you built the flywheel, skip the encoder everywhere it comes up. A flywheel only cares about speed, and the motor measures that by itself.
Order matters here. Power goes on first, then the USB cable. After that, Tuner X needs two settings changed, and neither one is a team number.
Step four is the one that bites later. The name you type has to match the code in every lesson that follows, so spell it exactly as it's shown.
A device in the list isn't proof of anything, because old firmware connects and answers just the same. Update the CANivore first, then everything else.
Once the flashing finishes, the card colours do the checking for you. Green is what you want on every card. Yellow means there's still an update waiting.
Red isn't a firmware problem at all. Two devices are answering to the same number, and that's the next lesson's job.
Now pull the battery and the USB, and bring both back. Nothing should be lost, since the name and the firmware live on the devices themselves.
On an arm there's one more test. Turn it by hand and watch the encoder's position change on screen. Everything's on the bus and current, so next, each device gets its own number.
